Flame in Freefall: AI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
Flame in Freefall is an interactive educational and research platform designed to explore how fire behaves in microgravity and how scientific insights can contribute to safer space missions.

The project addresses the challenge of understanding combustion under reduced gravity, where conventional buoyancy-driven airflow is weakened and flames can behave differently than on Earth.

We developed an interactive fire simulator that visualizes changes in flame behavior under different gravitational conditions, including Earth, the Moon, Mars, and microgravity. Users can adjust oxygen concentration, ventilation, and combustible materials to explore their effects on flame characteristics.

The platform also includes a NASA Data & Analysis section featuring preliminary combustion data visualizations, scientific explanations based on FLEX and BASS research, and a multilingual AI assistant designed to answer questions about spacecraft fire safety.

By combining scientific research, interactive visualization, and accessible learning tools, Flame in Freefall aims to improve understanding of combustion in space, encourage scientific exploration, and highlight the importance of fire safety for future human space missions.
details:
Flame in Freefall: An AI-Powered Platform for Exploring Combustion and Fire Safety in Space

1. Project Overview

Flame in Freefall is an interactive scientific and educational web platform that combines NASA combustion research, visual simulations, experimental data analysis, and artificial intelligence to explore fire behavior in microgravity.

The project addresses an important challenge in human space exploration: understanding how fire behaves in reduced-gravity environments and how this knowledge can contribute to safer spacecraft and future missions.

On Earth, buoyancy-driven convection causes hot gases to rise, influencing flame shape, heat transfer, and combustion processes. In microgravity, this natural convection is significantly reduced, changing flame geometry, oxygen transport, and the movement of combustion products.

Understanding these differences is essential for advancing spacecraft fire safety research, particularly as humanity prepares for longer missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

2. How Does Our Platform Work?

Flame in Freefall integrates several interconnected modules.

Interactive Fire Simulator

The platform features an interactive fire simulator that allows users to explore how environmental conditions can influence flame behavior.

Users can adjust:

  • Gravity: Microgravity, the Moon, Mars, and Earth.
  • Oxygen concentration: Different atmospheric oxygen levels.
  • Ventilation: Changes in airflow intensity.
  • Combustible materials: Gases, liquid fuels, and solid materials with different combustion characteristics.

The simulator displays animated flames whose visual characteristics change according to the selected parameters.

This provides an accessible way to explore combustion principles without conducting dangerous physical experiments.

The simulator is a qualitative educational visualization rather than a validated predictive combustion model.

NASA Data & Analysis

This module introduces users to NASA's experimental combustion research, particularly:

FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment): Investigates liquid fuel droplet combustion and flame extinction in microgravity.

BASS and BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids): Investigate combustion and flame spread over solid materials under reduced-gravity conditions, including the effects of ventilation.

The platform includes interactive graphs and tables presenting measurements of oxygen (O₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂), and carbon monoxide (CO).

A preliminary secondary dataset containing 20 BASS-II records is used for exploratory visualization. These numerical records require further verification against original NASA archives before they can support definitive scientific conclusions.

Flame Intelligence AI Assistant

The platform includes a multilingual AI assistant designed around the Google Gemini API.

The assistant is intended to help users understand combustion processes, microgravity, NASA experiments, oxygen concentration, ventilation, and spacecraft fire safety.

Its interface supports three languages: English, Russian, and Kazakh.

AI-generated explanations are presented as educational assistance rather than independently verified scientific findings.

Research & Methodology

This section presents the scientific problem, research hypothesis, objectives, methodology, and limitations of the project.

It explains how scientific literature, available experimental observations, exploratory data analysis, and educational visualization contribute to the platform.

Safety Insights

This module introduces key spacecraft fire safety considerations, including material flammability, oxygen availability, ventilation, fire detection, and suppression.

It connects scientific principles to the challenges of protecting astronauts and spacecraft during future missions.

3. Technologies and Development Tools

The platform was developed using accessible web technologies and scientific research resources.

HTML5 provides the structure of the website and its interconnected research modules.

CSS3 supports the responsive, space-inspired interface, including layouts suitable for computers and mobile devices.

JavaScript powers interactive controls, animated flame visualizations, language switching, and dynamic data presentation.

Chart.js is used to create interactive scientific graphs.

Google Gemini API provides the intended generative AI functionality for the scientific assistant.

GitHub supports source-code management and version control.

Vercel hosts the web platform and provides serverless functionality for communication with the AI service.

Microsoft Excel and CSV are used to organize and explore experimental data.

NASA scientific resources, particularly FLEX and BASS research materials, provide the scientific foundation for the project.

The platform is browser-based and does not require specialized hardware from its users.

4. Innovation and Creativity

The central innovation of Flame in Freefall is its integration of scientific research, interactive visualization, experimental data exploration, and artificial intelligence within a single accessible environment.

Rather than presenting scientific information only through static articles, the platform encourages users to actively investigate combustion concepts.

Visitors can modify gravity, oxygen concentration, ventilation, and material selection, observe qualitative changes in animated flames, examine experimental measurements, and explore scientific explanations.

The project also emphasizes the differences between combustion under terrestrial and reduced-gravity conditions.

Its multilingual design increases accessibility for international audiences, including students and early-career researchers.

By transforming complex combustion research into an interactive learning experience, Flame in Freefall offers a creative approach to communicating space science.

5. Factors Considered During Development

Several important principles guided the development process.

Scientific accuracy: The platform distinguishes established combustion principles and documented NASA research from preliminary observations and simplified visual simulations.

Accessibility: The website is designed to be accessible through standard web browsers and provides content in English, Russian, and Kazakh.

Interactivity: Users can independently explore how different environmental parameters influence conceptual flame behavior.

Safety: The platform allows combustion concepts to be studied without conducting physical fire experiments. It does not replace certified spacecraft safety systems or engineering assessments.

Data quality: Missing values, unusual measurements, and limitations of secondary experimental datasets are acknowledged rather than treated as verified scientific findings.

Scalability: The modular website architecture allows future integration of additional NASA datasets, improved physical models, and more advanced analytical tools.

6. Benefits and Intended Impact

Flame in Freefall aims to make NASA combustion research more understandable and accessible to a wider audience.

Its primary benefits include improving scientific literacy, supporting STEM education, encouraging experimental thinking, and demonstrating the importance of spacecraft fire safety.

Students and educators can use the simulator to explore how gravity, oxygen, ventilation, and fuel properties influence combustion behavior.

The data analysis module introduces users to experimental measurements and the importance of interpreting scientific information carefully.

The AI assistant is intended to make scientific explanations more accessible through multilingual question-and-answer interaction.

In the future, the platform could be expanded with additional verified NASA datasets, quantitative combustion models, uncertainty analysis, and improved comparisons between experimental observations and simulation results.

Although Flame in Freefall is not designed to control spacecraft fire protection systems or provide operational safety predictions, it can contribute to broader awareness and understanding of the scientific challenges associated with fire in space.

7. Conclusion

Flame in Freefall transforms complex microgravity combustion research into an accessible, interactive scientific learning platform.

By combining NASA research materials, animated simulations, exploratory data analysis, and artificial intelligence, the project creates opportunities for students, educators, and science enthusiasts to investigate the behavior of fire beyond Earth.

Our vision is to make space science more engaging, accessible, and understandable while inspiring the next generation of researchers to explore solutions for safer human space exploration.
